summary: Builds the people, partnerships, funding and operating infrastructure King’s needs to create high-quality experiential opportunities, connect students and graduates with employers in the UK and internationally, remove barriers to participation, and support successful transition into graduate futures.
detailSummary:
King’s already holds extensive relationships with employers, industry, public bodies, community and third-sector organisations, civic and cultural partners, international organisations and alumni. It also has strong careers expertise, pockets of student-opportunity funding, philanthropic relationships and locally developed processes for experiential activity. These assets are distributed across faculties and professional services and are not yet consistently visible, coordinated or activated as one coherent institutional engine for opportunity and graduate success.

The proposition therefore brings together four connected capabilities. First, King’s will preserve and strengthen the common operating infrastructure through which experiential opportunities are sourced, designed, approved, promoted, delivered, supported and evaluated. This includes clearer roles across central teams and faculties; proportionate standards for quality, accessibility, safeguarding, risk, data and student support; common templates and agreements; simpler contracting and payment routes; better partner intelligence; and a clearer institutional opportunity pipeline. Delivery remains distributed: the infrastructure should make local delivery easier, safer and more consistent rather than centralising it.

Second, King’s will create dedicated international employer-engagement capacity. The immediate phase will protect and deepen the existing East Asia portfolio through a G6 Employer Relations & Insights Manager and a G5 East Asia Adviser. From September 2027, two further G5 Advisers will extend capacity across South and South East Asia and Europe and North America. A £50,000 annual non-pay envelope will support employer-facing and in-country activity. This capability is intended to improve access to relevant employers and labour-market intelligence for students and graduates while also strengthening King’s employability proposition in strategically important recruitment markets.

Third, King’s will establish a small Graduate Transitions function from May 2027, initially comprising a G7 Head of Graduate Transitions and a G6 Graduate Transitions Coach. The function will move support beyond a predominantly reactive model by using Careers Readiness and other available data to identify graduates who may be at risk of poorer outcomes and provide targeted coaching, job-search support, employer referral and other interventions through the critical post-completion period captured by Graduate Outcomes.

Fourth, the deliverable will retain the existing access and opportunity-growth work. King’s will review and consolidate financial support for students undertaking employment-enhancing and developmental activity, with the intended direction of a coherent Student Opportunities Fund combining low-friction microbursaries of around £150-£250 with more substantial awards of around £4,000 for genuine out-of-pocket participation costs. Any new award pot sits outside the King’s Edge mobilisation ask and requires a separate institutional, consolidated-fund, philanthropic or other funding route. Alumni engagement and philanthropy will also be used deliberately to grow the supply of opportunity, including service-learning and social-good projects and models in which paid PhD project leads can mobilise flexible opportunities for wider student participation.

The causal logic is that King’s can create more meaningful and accessible experience, connect it more effectively to employers and graduate destinations, and improve institutional efficiency by joining up assets it already holds with a small number of targeted new capabilities. The enduring operating model should continue to respond to the demand generated by 2.1.4 Curriculum-Embedded Opportunity Growth and Assurance, 2.2.3 Near-Curriculum Pathways and 2.2.4 Flexible Adjunct Experiential and Thematic Opportunities. The specified £390,354 annualised new-resource package is the current Core ask for the international and graduate-transition capabilities. It does not pre-approve any additional experiential-infrastructure staffing beyond existing and repurposed capacity; any further requirement should be evidenced through delivery.

caseForChange.problem: King’s has substantial external relationships, careers expertise, alumni connection and pockets of student-opportunity funding, but the infrastructure that turns these assets into opportunity and positive graduate destinations is fragmented. Relationship management, opportunity design, contracting, risk, payments, partner intelligence, international employer engagement, graduate support and financial-access mechanisms can operate separately. This creates duplicated effort, missed connections, uneven access, fragile international capability and a reactive transition model for graduates who need additional support.
caseForChange.opportunity: King’s can create a stronger institutional engine that connects experiential opportunity infrastructure, employer relationships, international labour-market capability, proactive graduate transition, alumni engagement, philanthropy and student financial support. Shared operating standards can reduce friction and duplication without centralising delivery. Dedicated international employer capacity can protect and expand strategically valuable relationships. A small Graduate Transitions function can target support where it is most needed. A coherent Student Opportunities Fund and philanthropic propositions can remove financial barriers and grow opportunity supply.
caseForChange.whyNow: King’s Edge is increasing the volume and ambition of experiential opportunity within and beyond the curriculum at the same time as the graduate labour market becomes more challenging and employability becomes more important to student choice. Existing East Asia employability activity has demonstrated value but is unsupported by dedicated resource and has displaced domestic employer-engagement capacity. Graduate support remains largely reactive after completion. Universities UK’s Future Jobs Roadmap also makes easier employer engagement with universities an explicit part of the national response. Building the operating infrastructure now allows King’s to protect valuable relationships, strengthen graduate transition and scale opportunity before fragmented processes become a constraint on programme ambition.
caseForChange.intendedChange: King’s moves from fragmented relationship, opportunity, funding and graduate-transition activity towards connected employability and experiential infrastructure. Staff and partners work through clearer routes and common processes; students have more consistent access to meaningful experience and financial support; employer engagement is stronger in the UK and priority international markets; graduates at greater risk of poorer outcomes can be identified and supported proactively; and King’s can evidence both Education and Student Success benefits and wider recruitment and reputation benefits from the same institutional capability.

problemSolved: King’s does not yet consistently convert its distributed external relationships, employability capability, alumni connection and opportunity funding into a coherent supply of accessible experience and sustained support through the transition into graduate destinations.
whatChanges: King’s establishes connected experiential, employer-engagement, access and graduate-transition infrastructure that can generate and sustain more opportunities, reduce operational friction, remove financial barriers, strengthen international employer connection and intervene proactively where graduates need additional support.
